docs.title: How work flows here
docs.text:
1. Log in to master — prepare scripts and inputs there
  2. Check sinfo / squeue — see what's free before you plan
  3. Submit with sbatch — declare CPUs, memory, time, GPU
  4. Compute on node1–node3 or gpunode1 — never on master
  5. Save results to durable NFS — scratch is not storage

About this handbook

This handbook contains infrastructure evidence and is intended for authorised lab users. Do not publish it publicly or share it outside approved channels. Read the documentation status policy before copying pages into another system.

docs.title: Before requesting help
docs.text:
Capture enough evidence for another person to understand the issue without guessing:

hostname
date
sinfo
squeue -u "$USER"
df -hT

Include the command you ran, the complete error message, the affected path or job ID, and what changed immediately before the problem began. Never include a password, token, private key, or sensitive research data in a support request.

docs.title: Best Practices That Prevent Bad Days
docs.text:
Best practices are not ceremonial rules. They are shortcuts around failures the lab does not want to experience twice: lost data, frozen login sessions, unusable GPUs, irreproducible results, and weekend recovery work.

This section explains what to do, why it matters, and what failure it prevents in the Functional Genomics Lab HPC environment.

The standard

A good practice should make the safe action easier, make mistakes visible, and let a junior operator recover without guessing.

docs.title: Choose your path
docs.text: If you are... Start here You will avoid... A new student Researcher workflow running analysis on master, misplaced data, unreproducible jobs Starting a project Storage decisions full filesystems, slow pipelines, lost scratch data Writing jobs Reliable Slurm jobs oversubscription, unexplained pending jobs, missing logs Using accelerators Responsible GPU use blocking both V100 GPUs with a poorly sized job On operational duty Calm operations risky multi-change recovery and undocumented fixes Investigating an alert Evidence-first troubleshooting changing the wrong subsystem Planning maintenance Hardware, network, and backups avoidable outages and unrecoverable changes

docs.title: What are you protecting?
docs.text: Asset Best practice Why it matters Research data Know the storage tier and backup boundary A mounted filesystem is not automatically a backup Reproducibility Save job scripts, parameters, and software versions Six months later, memory is not a method section Shared capacity Request what the job uses One oversized request can delay everyone Cluster stability Keep computation off master The controller must remain responsive to schedule and recover jobs Recovery time Change one thing, then validate Multiple simultaneous changes destroy cause-and-effect evidence Institutional knowledge Update this handbook after real incidents Chat history is not an operational record

docs.title: The five habits
docs.text:
1. Place work deliberately. Choose storage, CPU, memory, and GPU resources based on workload behavior.
  2. Use Slurm for computation. Interactive login is for preparation, not production analysis.
  3. Make results reproducible. Keep scripts, logs, versions, and parameters with the project.
  4. Validate boundaries. Confirm mounts, time, services, and node state before assuming an application is broken.
  5. Leave the cluster easier to understand. Clean scratch, explain changes, and improve the runbook that helped you.

docs.title: A useful test
docs.text:
Before doing something unusual, ask:

If this fails tonight, will another person know what I changed, where the important data lives, and how to return the cluster to a known-good state?

If the answer is no, improve the plan before running the command.

docs.title: Backups You Can Actually Restore
docs.text: A backup is not a copy command that once succeeded. It is a tested path from a bad event to a usable recovery.

docs.title: Start with failure, not software
docs.text:
Different failures need different protection:

Failure Protection needed Accidental deletion versioned or snapshot-based recovery Filesystem corruption independent copy outside the affected filesystem Disk or pool failure redundancy plus backup Master loss configuration, state, documentation, and rebuild procedure Ransomware or privileged mistake isolated/offline or immutable copy Scientific irreproducibility scripts, metadata, references, and versions

RAID and ZFS mirrors reduce interruption from device failure. They also mirror deletion and corruption. Availability is not historical recovery.

docs.title: Define the promise per storage tier
docs.text:
Users must know what is protected:

  • /home: which files, frequency, retention, and restore contact
  • /nfs_master: which active projects qualify and how versions are retained
  • /Fungel: which archives are independently protected
  • local NVMe and /DATA: normally disposable unless explicitly staged out
  • cluster configuration: enough material to rebuild services and trust

Ambiguity loses data

If a student believes scratch is backed up while administrators believe it is disposable, the backup design has already failed.

docs.title: Back up operational knowledge
docs.text:
Preserve more than data:

  • this repository and its history
  • /etc configurations for Slurm, MUNGE, Chrony, NFS, AutoFS, networking, and relevant systemd overrides
  • package, kernel, driver, firmware, and hardware inventory
  • Slurm state and accounting material where applicable
  • storage layout, UUIDs, exports, permissions, and recovery dependencies
  • encryption or credential recovery material under appropriate controls

Why: terabytes of intact data are difficult to use if nobody can reconstruct the identities, mounts, permissions, and services around them.

docs.title: Test restores, not backup logs
docs.text:
Periodically restore:

  1. one ordinary user file
  2. one project directory with permissions
  3. one configuration file to an isolated location
  4. one larger dataset sample
  5. one documented disaster scenario

Measure recovery time and compare checksums, ownership, ACLs, and usability.

docs.title: A backup review should answer
docs.text:
• What is included and excluded?
  • How old can the recovered copy be?
  • How long will restoration take?
  • Who can authorize and perform it?
  • Is the copy independent of the original failure domain?
  • When did a restore last succeed?

Until those answers are tested, the cluster has a backup hope—not a backup capability.

docs.title: Make Two GPUs Serve a Whole Lab
docs.text: gpunode1 contains two Tesla V100 PCIe 32 GB GPUs. That makes GPU time valuable, but it does not make every workload faster.

docs.title: Why deliberate GPU use matters
docs.text: A CPU-only program placed on the GPU node occupies scarce scheduling capacity without using the accelerators. An oversized GPU request can block both devices. A job that repeatedly reloads terabytes over NFS may spend more time waiting for data than computing.

docs.title: Use the GPU when the application can prove it
docs.text:
Good candidates include:

  • CUDA-enabled deep-learning training or inference
  • GPU-enabled bioinformatics applications
  • supported protein-structure or image-analysis workflows
  • workloads benchmarked faster on V100 hardware

Do not choose gpu because the node sounds more powerful. Compare runtime, throughput, and total resource occupancy against a CPU run.

docs.title: The allocation contract
docs.text:
• Request GPUs explicitly through Slurm.
  • Request one GPU unless the software genuinely scales across two.
  • Match CPU and memory requests to preprocessing needs.
  • Keep unrelated CPU-only stages off the GPU allocation.
  • Capture nvidia-smi and software-version information in diagnostic logs.

Visibility is a startup gate

Both /dev/nvidia0 and /dev/nvidia1 must exist and both V100 devices must appear in nvidia-smi before slurmd returns gpunode1 to service.

docs.title: Feed the accelerator efficiently
docs.text:
Stage reusable or high-I/O temporary data to local /DATA when appropriate, then copy final outputs to shared storage. This reduces NFS pressure and keeps the GPU from waiting on avoidable data transfers.

/DATA is local working storage—not the durable source of truth and not a BeeGFS target.

docs.title: After driver or CUDA changes
docs.text:
Validate in this order:

  1. PCI devices are visible.
  2. NVIDIA kernel modules are loaded.
  3. nvidia-smi reports both GPUs without errors.
  4. Slurm GRES configuration matches detected devices.
  5. A small scheduled GPU test succeeds.
  6. Only then allow production workloads.

Why: checking nvidia-smi alone proves the driver can see hardware; a scheduled test proves users can access it through the actual Slurm path.

docs.title: Fair-use outcome
docs.text: A good GPU job uses the accelerator substantially, releases it promptly, leaves reproducible logs, and does not make the next researcher clean its temporary data.

docs.title: Performance Is a Placement Decision
docs.text: Fast hardware cannot rescue a workflow that reads from the wrong storage tier, requests unused CPUs, or leaves a GPU waiting for data. Most practical HPC performance comes from matching work to the resource that limits it.

docs.title: Find the bottleneck before tuning
docs.text:
Observation Likely limit Useful response CPUs mostly idle, I/O wait high storage or data layout stage locally, reduce small-file operations Memory pressure or OOM working-set size request/choose adequate memory, reduce concurrency More threads stop helping serial work or contention use the measured efficient thread count GPU utilization low input pipeline or CPU preprocessing stage data, tune loaders, right-size CPUs One worker is slower node-local drift compare hardware, thermals, mounts, and configuration

Tuning without measurement often moves complexity rather than improving throughput.

docs.title: Optimize the whole workflow
docs.text: A 20% faster alignment step may not matter if sorting, compression, and shared storage dominate runtime. Measure stage durations and optimize the longest or most repeated constraint.

docs.title: CPU jobs
docs.text:
• Match application threads to allocated CPUs.
  • Benchmark representative thread counts; twice the threads rarely means twice the speed.
  • Consider total throughput: two efficient jobs may finish more samples than one oversized job.
  • Keep memory bandwidth and NUMA effects in mind for large in-memory workloads.

docs.title: I/O-heavy jobs
docs.text:
• Stage temporary random-I/O work to local NVMe or scratch.
  • Combine pathological collections of tiny files when the format permits.
  • Avoid every array task downloading or copying the same reference.
  • Copy only durable outputs back to shared storage.

docs.title: GPU jobs
docs.text:
• Measure utilization rather than assuming acceleration.
  • Keep data preparation from starving the GPU.
  • Request two GPUs only when scaling is demonstrated.
  • Compare time-to-result and GPU-hours, not just one kernel's speed.

docs.title: Benchmark like an experiment
docs.text:
Record:

  • input dataset and checksum
  • software, kernel, driver, and firmware versions
  • job resources and node
  • storage source and destination
  • elapsed time, CPU efficiency, peak memory, and I/O
  • temperatures or throttling where relevant

Change one variable and compare against a known-good baseline. A benchmark without context becomes a number nobody can reproduce.

docs.title: The useful outcome
docs.text: Performance work should increase completed science per day without reducing fairness, reliability, or reproducibility. A fragile one-off speed record is not an operational improvement.

docs.title: Slurm Jobs That Explain Themselves
docs.text: Slurm is not an inconvenience between a researcher and a server. It is the agreement that keeps shared CPUs, memory, and GPUs predictable.

docs.title: Why Slurm discipline matters
docs.text: Without the scheduler, one process can consume a node's memory, another can take all CPU threads, and neither user has a reliable record of what happened. With Slurm, resource ownership, logs, job state, and failure reasons are visible.

docs.title: A trustworthy job requests what it uses
docs.text:
Resource Request based on Why CPUs the tool's effective thread count Extra CPUs sit idle while other jobs wait Memory measured peak plus a reasonable margin Too little kills jobs; too much blocks scheduling Time observed runtime plus uncertainty Huge time limits weaken queue planning GPU explicit accelerator need and count gpunode1 has only two shared V100 GPUs

The thread-count contract

If Slurm allocates 16 CPUs, configure the application for 16 threads. Asking for 32 and using 4 wastes 28 CPUs; asking for 4 and launching 32 overloads the node.

docs.title: Make every job auditable
docs.text:
A production job script should make these visible:

  • project and purpose in the job name
  • partition and requested resources
  • explicit output and error paths
  • working directory
  • loaded modules or activated environment
  • exact application command and parameters
  • stage-in, stage-out, and cleanup behavior

Keep the submitted script with the project even after the job finishes. Slurm logs explain execution; the script explains intent.

docs.title: Read state before reacting
docs.text: Symptom First question Why Job is pending What does the pending reason say? It may be waiting normally for resources Job is out of memory What was peak memory use? Re-running unchanged repeats the failure Node is drained What reason did Slurm record? Resume without fixing the cause hides evidence Job fails immediately Did environment/setup complete? The application may never have started GPU job sees no GPU Was a GPU actually requested? Login-shell visibility is not an allocation

docs.title: User standard
docs.text:
1. Test small inputs first.
  2. Submit through compute or gpu as appropriate.
  3. Monitor resource efficiency after representative runs.
  4. Adjust requests using evidence.
  5. Preserve the script and logs with results.

docs.title: Administrator standard
docs.text:
• Keep master responsive and free of production computation.
  • Investigate DOWN, DRAIN, INVALID_REG, and repeated failures before issuing RESUME.
  • Keep /etc/slurm/slurm.conf consistent across the controller and workers.
  • Validate MUNGE, time, network, mounts, and slurmd before blaming scheduling.
  • Prefer simple partitions until a demonstrated policy requires complexity.

The best scheduler configuration is not the most sophisticated one. It is the one users can request correctly and operators can explain under pressure.

docs.title: Put Data Where It Belongs
docs.text: On a genomics cluster, storage choice affects speed, recoverability, and every other user. A FASTQ file in the wrong place is not merely untidy—it can fill a critical filesystem or turn one pipeline into cluster-wide I/O contention.

docs.title: The decision in one table
docs.text:
Location Put this here Do not rely on it for Why /nvme + /nvme_vf (BeeGFS) alignments, sorting, decompression, pipeline intermediates — shared across all nodes the only copy of a result Fastest shared tier (23.7 TB parallel scratch), but disposable /home shell configuration, scripts, notebooks, small personal files raw runs, BAM/CRAM collections, large environments Home must stay responsive for login and AutoFS access /nfs_master active projects, shared inputs, workflow outputs unlimited archival growth It is the working data area seen by compute nodes /Fungel large shared datasets, curated references, archives uncontrolled temporary output Capacity is valuable and already heavily used CPU-node NVMe/local scratch sorting, indexing, decompression, temporary intermediates the only copy of a result Fast and local, but disposable gpunode1:/DATA GPU-local staging and temporary work durable shared storage It exists only on the GPU node

Mounted does not mean backed up

NFS, ZFS, RAID, and large disks improve availability in different ways. None automatically creates a recoverable historical copy of deleted or corrupted research data.

docs.title: Why tiering improves performance
docs.text:
Many genomics tools create temporary files much larger than their final output. If thousands of small operations run directly against NFS, latency and metadata traffic affect everyone. Staging those intermediates locally lets the node use its own disks while shared storage carries only inputs and final outputs.

The safe pattern is:

shared input → scratch (BeeGFS /nvme or node-local) → computation → shared final result

The unsafe pattern is:

only copy → local scratch → reboot → lost result

docs.title: A project layout people can understand
docs.text:
/nfs_master/projects/PROJECT/
├── README.md
├── raw/          # immutable or read-only inputs
├── metadata/
├── workflow/
├── jobs/
├── logs/
├── results/
└── archive-manifest.txt

Separate raw inputs from generated results. A cleanup command should never need to guess which files came from the sequencer and which can be regenerated.

docs.title: Rules with reasons
docs.text: Practice Failure prevented Keep raw data immutable Accidental pipeline overwrites Share one curated reference copy Wasted capacity and inconsistent analyses Monitor inodes as well as bytes “Disk has space” failures caused by millions of files Use project groups and controlled permissions Private data exposure and collaboration failures Define retention before producing data Emergency deletion when a filesystem reaches 100% Verify copy completion before deleting scratch Silent partial-result loss

docs.title: Before a large run
docs.text:
• Estimate input, temporary, and final-output size separately.
  • Confirm the destination mount with findmnt -T PATH.
  • Confirm adequate free space and inodes.
  • Decide what must survive and where it will be copied.
  • Add cleanup only after successful stage-out.

docs.title: Administrator perspective
docs.text: Capacity alerts are late signals. Review growth trends, unusually large directories, and repeated scratch leakage before users begin seeing write failures. When changing mounts, validate the source—not only that the path exists—because an unmounted empty directory can look deceptively healthy.

docs.title: A Researcher Workflow That Scales
docs.text: The cluster works best when researchers separate preparing work, running work, and keeping results. Mixing those stages is the fastest route to a slow login node and confusing projects.

docs.title: Why you should care
docs.text:
A workflow that runs correctly once can still be a poor cluster workflow. If it depends on shell history, writes terabytes into /home, or runs outside Slurm, it becomes difficult to reproduce, share, schedule, or support.

The master node is not a workstation

Use master to inspect files, edit scripts, submit jobs, and review results. A large analysis on master competes with Slurm, authentication, NFS, and every other user trying to access the cluster.

docs.title: 1. Enter through master
docs.text:
Use master for lightweight work:

  • editing a job script
  • checking small text files
  • loading an environment to verify a command
  • submitting and monitoring Slurm jobs

Move to a compute allocation before testing anything CPU-, memory-, or I/O-intensive.

docs.title: 2. Give the project a durable home
docs.text:
Create one recognizable project directory on /nfs_master or the agreed shared project area. Keep these together:

project/
├── README.md
├── config/
├── jobs/
├── logs/
├── results/
└── workflow/

Why: when scripts and logs live beside results, collaborators can understand how an output was produced without reconstructing your terminal history.

docs.title: 3. Submit computation through Slurm
docs.text:
• CPU analysis goes to the compute partition.
  • GPU analysis goes to the gpu partition.
  • Requested CPUs must match tool threads.
  • Requested memory must reflect measured use, not guesswork.

Why: Slurm prevents two users from silently consuming the same CPUs, memory, or GPUs and gives administrators evidence when something fails.

docs.title: 4. Use scratch for temporary pressure
docs.text:
Stage large temporary files to node-local storage when the tool creates heavy random I/O. Copy final results back to shared storage before the job exits.

Why: scratch protects shared filesystems from avoidable traffic, but it can be lost during reboot, cleanup, or hardware maintenance.

docs.title: 5. Leave evidence
docs.text:
For any result used in a report or publication, retain:

  • the submitted job script
  • software and reference versions
  • input locations or checksums
  • parameters and random seeds
  • Slurm output/error logs
  • a short interpretation of the result

docs.title: Habits that save hours
docs.text: Habit Why it helps Name projects and runs consistently Makes storage review and collaboration possible Reuse curated references Avoids duplicated storage and reference-version drift Review squeue reasons Pending is often a resource request problem, not a broken cluster Clean scratch in job cleanup logic Prevents local disks filling weeks later Ask before changing shared software Protects every workflow depending on the current version

docs.title: Ask for help when
docs.text:
• a shared mount is missing, read-only, or unexpectedly empty
  • a job repeatedly fails before executing your command
  • a GPU is not visible inside a valid allocation
  • permissions prevent legitimate project collaboration
  • resource use is much larger than expected

Bring the job ID, job script, log path, and exact error. “It did not work” is a symptom; those four items make it diagnosable.

docs.title: GPU
docs.text: The GPU node is a specialized shared resource and usually needs clearer policy than CPU nodes.

docs.title: This section should explain
docs.text:
• installed GPU model and count
  • driver and toolkit expectations
  • how users request GPU resources in Slurm
  • how utilization and health are checked
  • common causes of GPU job failure

docs.title: Operator note
docs.text: GPU problems are often visible first as user complaints about jobs failing or waiting forever. Good monitoring and clear request examples reduce both.

docs.title: Local storage note
docs.text: gpunode1 currently exposes local /DATA storage rather than local NVMe scratch. Treat it as node-local working storage, not durable shared storage and not a BeeGFS storage target.

The one rule, repeated

Anything on scratch (/nvme*, node-local /DATA) can be deleted at any time. The only copy that survives is the one on shared NFS storage.

What does the cluster look like?

The full hardware map, network topology and inventory live in the Admin Zone — they are maintenance documentation, not required reading for running science.

docs.title: Submit Your First Slurm Job
docs.text:
First inspect the scheduler before choosing resources:

sinfo
squeue

Create a small test script named hello.slurm:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --job-name=hello
#SBATCH --output=hello-%j.out
#SBATCH --time=00:05:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=1G

hostname
date

Submit and monitor it:

sbatch hello.slurm
squeue --me

When the job completes, read the output file and review resource use:

cat hello-JOB_ID.out
sacct -j JOB_ID --format=JobID,State,Elapsed,AllocCPUS,MaxRSS

Replace JOB_ID with the numeric value returned by sbatch. Request only the CPU, memory, time, and GPU resources your workload needs. For a job that does not start or finishes unexpectedly, consult the Slurm reference and contact the administrator with the job ID and output file.

Next: return to the Getting Started overview.

docs.title: Connect to the Cluster
docs.text:
Connect to the master node first — never log directly into a compute node for normal work.

🪟 Windows🍎 macOS🐧 Linux
  1. Open PowerShell (search Start → “pwsh” or “PowerShell”).
  2. Run: 
    ssh USERNAME@master
  3. First time? Type yes at the host-key prompt.
  4. Password does not echo while typing — type it and press Enter.
Want tabs, saved sessions, file transfer?

Install Windows Terminal (free, from Microsoft Store) and optionally WinSCP for drag-and-drop file transfer.

  1. Open Terminal (Spotlight → “terminal”).
  2. Run: 
    ssh USERNAME@master
  3. First time? Type yes at the host-key prompt, then your password.

Open a terminal and run:

ssh USERNAME@master

Verify the host key fingerprint with the administrator before accepting it on first use.

After logging in, orient yourself:

hostname   # should say master
pwd        # you are in your home directory

master is a login and management node: prepare files and submit jobs here, but never run computational analysis on it — that is what the compute nodes are for.

Next: choose storage → load software → generate your first job.

docs.title: Use Environment Modules
docs.text:
Environment Modules select the software versions used by your shell and Slurm jobs. Check the available modules before relying on a package name or version.

module avail
module spider PACKAGE_NAME
module load PACKAGE_NAME/VERSION
module list

To remove a module from the current shell:

module unload PACKAGE_NAME

Put the same module load commands in your Slurm job script so the job runs with the intended software environment. If the needed package is absent, ask the administrator before installing system-wide software.

Next: submit your first Slurm job.

docs.title: Choose the Right Storage Location
docs.text:
Use shared storage for data that must survive beyond one job. Use node-local storage only for temporary working files that can be recreated.

Location Use for Do not use for /home scripts, configuration, and small personal files large datasets or heavy job output /nfs_master active project data and workflow outputs disposable high-I/O intermediates /Fungel large shared datasets and references temporary job scratch node-local /DATA or NVMe recreatable, high-I/O intermediate files the only copy of important data

Before starting a job, check available capacity on the filesystem you intend to use:

df -hT /home /nfs_master /Fungel

The full storage overview explains which paths are shared, which are local to a worker, and how they are mounted.

Next: load software with environment modules.

docs.title: 🛠️ Slurm job script generator
docs.text:
Answer six questions, get a correct, commented sbatch script. The preview below updates as you type. Copy it (or download it), edit the command block, submit. When in doubt, over-asking slightly is better than a job that gets cancelled.

Job name Partitioncompute (default)gpu — ask admin first (currently inactive) CPUs per task Memory per node (GB) Time limit (hours) GPUs01 (V100-32GB)2 (V100-32GB) Software modules (hold ⌘/Ctrl to pick several) STAR/2.7.11bsamtools/1.24fastp/v1.0.1 fastqc/0.12.1multiqc/v1.31trim_galore/0.6.10 cutadapt/5.2bwa-mem2-2.3minimap2/2.30 kallisto/0.51.1cellranger/10.1.0spaceranger/4.1.0 gatk/4.6.2.0picard/v3.4.0bedtools2/2.31.1 blast-suite/2.17.0rmats-turbo/v4.3.0 python/3.11.9R/4.6.1nextflow/25.04.7 singularity/4.3.2gromacs/2025kraken2/2.1.6 parallelpigz/2.8 Your commands # example: # STAR --runThreadN 8 --genomeDir /path/to/star_index --readFilesIn R1.fq.gz R2.fq.gz ... 📋 Copy script ⬇ Download job.sh
How to use the script you just copied

Save it as job.sh, put your data on shared storage, then:

sbatch job.sh        # submit
squeue -u "$USER"    # watch it

docs.title: Slurm: Jobs, Queue, and Free Nodes
docs.text:
Use Slurm commands from master to see the live cluster state. The output of these commands is the source of truth at the moment you run them; do not rely on an old inventory report for job availability.

Do not run analysis on master

Use master to inspect Slurm, prepare files, and submit jobs. Run compute workloads through Slurm on the execution nodes.

docs.title: Fast status check
docs.text:
Run these three commands first:

sinfo
squeue
squeue -u "$USER"
Command Shows sinfo partitions and how many nodes are idle, allocated, mixed, or unavailable squeue all jobs that are running or waiting squeue -u "$USER" only your jobs

docs.title: See the current jobs and queue
docs.text:
Use this readable queue format:

squeue -o '%.12i %.12P %.24j %.12u %.2t %.10M %.6D %R'

The columns mean: job ID, partition, job name, user, state, elapsed time, number of nodes, and allocated node or pending reason.

Illustrative example only — not live cluster output:

       JOBID    PARTITION                     NAME         USER ST    TIME  NODES NODELIST(REASON)
        1842          cpu                rnaseq-align       maya  R    18:42      1 node1
        1843          gpu                 train-model      arun PD     0:00      1 (Resources)

In this example, job 1842 is running on node1. Job 1843 is waiting because the requested resources are not currently available.

docs.title: Show only waiting jobs
docs.text:
squeue --states=PENDING -o '%.12i %.12P %.24j %.12u %.10M %.6D %R'

The final column is important. Common reasons are:

Reason Meaning What to do Resources Requested CPU, memory, GPU, or node resources are busy Wait, or reduce a request only if your workload permits it Priority Other jobs are ahead in the scheduler order Wait; do not repeatedly resubmit the same job ReqNodeNotAvail A requested node is unavailable, down, or drained Remove an unnecessary node constraint or contact an administrator QOS... or Assoc... A policy, account, or quality-of-service rule applies Contact the administrator with the job ID

docs.title: See when a waiting job may start
docs.text:
Ask Slurm for an estimated start time for your pending jobs:

squeue --start -u "$USER"

For one job:

squeue --start --jobs JOB_ID
scontrol show job JOB_ID

squeue --start is an estimate, not a promise. It can change when jobs finish, new work is submitted, reservations change, or resource requests change. If no estimate is available, inspect the Reason= field from scontrol show job.

Check scheduled reservations, if the cluster uses them:

scontrol show reservation

docs.title: See free and busy nodes
docs.text:
Start with the partition summary:

sinfo -o '%P %a %l %D %t %C %G'

Illustrative example only — not live cluster output:

PARTITION AVAIL TIMELIMIT NODES STATE CPUS(A/I/O/T) GRES
cpu*         up 2-00:00:00     2 idle 0/256/0/256   (null)
gpu          up 2-00:00:00     1 mix  32/96/0/128   gpu:2
  • idle means the node has no allocated Slurm resources.
  • mix means some resources are allocated and some remain available.
  • alloc means all schedulable resources are allocated.
  • down, drain, or drng mean the node is unavailable for new work.
  • CPUS(A/I/O/T) means allocated, idle, other, and total CPUs.

List individual nodes and their resources:

sinfo -N -o '%N %T %c %m %G %E'

To show only fully idle nodes:

sinfo --states=idle -N

To investigate unavailable nodes or scheduler notes:

sinfo -R
scontrol show node NODE_NAME

Replace NODE_NAME with a name shown by sinfo, such as node1 or gpunode1.

docs.title: Check GPU availability
docs.text:
First list the partitions that actually exist:

sinfo

If gpu is shown as a partition, inspect it with:

sinfo -p gpu
squeue -p gpu

Do not assume the partition is named gpu; use the exact partition name shown by sinfo.

docs.title: Follow one job
docs.text:
squeue -j JOB_ID
scontrol show job JOB_ID

After it finishes, accounting information may be available with:

sacct -j JOB_ID --format=JobID,JobName,State,Elapsed,AllocCPUS,ReqMem,MaxRSS

If sacct returns no data, accounting may not yet be configured or the record may not be available immediately after job completion.

docs.title: Handy daily commands
docs.text:
# My running and waiting jobs
squeue -u "$USER"

# All jobs with useful columns
squeue -o '%.12i %.12P %.24j %.12u %.2t %.10M %.6D %R'

# Only jobs waiting in the queue
squeue --states=PENDING

# Partition and node capacity summary
sinfo

# Individual node state and resources
sinfo -N -o '%N %T %c %m %G %E'

# Reasons for down or drained nodes
sinfo -R

For your first submission, follow the first Slurm job guide. Planned maintenance and recovery runbooks are maintained by the cluster admin — expect advance notice on the lab channel.

docs.title: FGHPC Storage
docs.text:
FGHPC combines large shared filesystems on master with high-capacity local disks and NVMe devices on the execution nodes, and a BeeGFS parallel scratch filesystem spread across the compute nodes' NVMe. The same pathname can therefore mean very different things operationally: durable shared data, an AutoFS view, shared scratch, or disposable node-local working space.

Current production state

Durable shared storage uses NFSv4 and AutoFS over dedicated ConnectX-5 links. BeeGFS is deployed (September 2026) as the cluster's parallel scratch tier: two filesystems — /nvme (21 TB) and /nvme_vf (2.7 TB) — backed by the NVMe of node1–node3, with management and metadata on master. Clients are live on master and gpunode1; client mounts on node1–node3 are still being finalized. BeeGFS is scratch: fast and shared, but disposable — never the only copy of your data.

docs.title: Storage at a glance
docs.text:
Tier Location Capacity in inventory Visible from Primary purpose BeeGFS parallel scratch /nvme + /nvme_vf (NVMe of node1–node3) 23.7 TB all nodes as BeeGFS clients high-throughput intermediates: alignments, sorting, pipeline temp files User homes master:/home, ZFS pool homefs 3.4 TiB usable master and workers through per-user AutoFS user configuration, scripts, small files Active shared data master:/nfs_master 174 TiB all workers through NFS active projects and workflow outputs Large shared data master:/Fungel 212 TiB all workers through NFS large datasets, references, archive-oriented storage Shared applications master:/apps part of 1.8 TiB root filesystem workers at /nfsroot/apps through AutoFS centrally managed software and modules CPU-node local RAID /DATA about 73 TiB per CPU node that node only large temporary or node-local work CPU-node local NVMe /NVME_DATA1, /NVME_DATA2 about 3.5 TiB each that node only high-I/O intermediates CPU-node local NVMe /NVME_DATA3 about 916 GiB that node only additional local working space GPU-node local data gpunode1:/DATA about 7.3 TiB gpunode1 only GPU-local staging and temporary data

Capacities and utilization are inventory snapshots, not quotas or guarantees. Always check live values before starting a large workflow.

docs.title: How data reaches a job
docs.text:
master
     ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
     │ ZFS /home                         │
     │ ext4 /nfs_master                  │
     │ ext4 /Fungel                      │
     │ XFS / containing /apps            │
     └───────────────┬───────────────────┘
                     │ NFSv4 / AutoFS
          dedicated 192.168.x.0/24 links
                     │
       ┌─────────────┼─────────────┬─────────────┐
       │             │             │             │
     node1         node2         node3       gpunode1
   shared mounts + local RAID/NVMe         shared mounts + local /DATA

The master copy is authoritative for shared paths. Local worker storage is not automatically synchronized to any other node.

BeeGFS adds a second, parallel scratch tier on top of the NFS tree. Its management and metadata services run on master; the actual bytes live on the NVMe of node1–node3, and every node mounts it as a client:

        master (management + metadata)
                    │
   ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
   │                │                │
 node1            node2            node3
 NVMe storage     NVMe storage     NVMe storage
   └────────────────┴────────────────┘
                    │
        striped namespace, mounted by all nodes
        /nvme  (21 TB)   +   /nvme_vf  (2.7 TB)

Use /nvme and /nvme_vf for the fast, throwaway middle of a workflow — intermediates, sorting, alignment — and keep the only durable copy on NFS.

docs.title: Choose the right page
docs.text:
• Shared storage: how /home, /nfs_master, /Fungel, and /apps are built and exported.
  • Local worker storage: exact /DATA and NVMe layout by node.
  • BeeGFS scratch (/nvme, /nvme_vf): parallel, shared, disposable — see data placement for what belongs there.
  • Mount architecture: NFS sources, AutoFS behavior, dependencies, and validation.
  • Capacity and health (monitored by the admin; ask if your job feels slow), ZFS, NVMe, and failure boundaries.
  • Storage recovery: safe diagnosis after reboot or mount failure.
  • Storage best practices: where researchers should place data and why.

docs.title: Fast live check
docs.text:
fghpc storage
df -hT
df -ih
findmnt -T /home
findmnt -T /nfs_master
findmnt -T /Fungel
findmnt -T /apps
findmnt -T /nvme
beegfs-df
fghpc beegfs

On workers, trigger AutoFS using a real child path such as /home/USERNAME or /nfsroot/apps; checking only /home does not prove a user's NFS mount works.

docs.title: Local Worker Storage
docs.text:
Worker-local storage accelerates jobs and absorbs temporary I/O. It is visible only on that host and is not automatically copied to shared storage.

Local means local

A result left only under /DATA or /NVME_DATA* can become unavailable when that worker is down and may be lost during repair, reformatting, or cleanup.

docs.title: CPU-node layout
docs.text:
All three CPU workers contain the same logical tiers, although Linux NVMe device numbers differ by host.

Mountpoint Approximate size Filesystem Intended use /DATA 73 TiB ext4 on RAID-controller virtual disk large node-local staging and intermediates /NVME_DATA1 3.5 TiB ext4 high-I/O temporary work /NVME_DATA2 3.5 TiB ext4 high-I/O temporary work /NVME_DATA3 916 GiB ext4 additional local working space / about 898 GiB XFS on separate 1 TB NVMe operating system; not project scratch

docs.title: Device-to-mount mapping
docs.text:
Do not copy raw /dev/nvmeXnY assumptions between workers:

Host Root device /NVME_DATA1 /NVME_DATA2 /NVME_DATA3 node1 nvme0n1p4 nvme2n1p1 nvme3n1p1 nvme1n1p1 node2 nvme2n1p4 nvme1n1 nvme0n1 nvme3n1 node3 nvme2n1p4 nvme0n1 nvme1n1 nvme3n1

Use filesystem UUIDs and mountpoints for persistent configuration. NVMe numbering is a discovery result, not a storage identity.

docs.title: Inventory utilization snapshot
docs.text:
Host /DATA /NVME_DATA1 /NVME_DATA2 /NVME_DATA3 node1 78% 66% 1% 1% node2 85% 1% 1% 1% node3 92% 4% 11% 1%

node3:/DATA was already near a critical threshold. These values change; use them as evidence of cleanup risk, not current truth.

docs.title: GPU-node layout
docs.text:
gpunode1 has no NVMe devices in the inventory. Its local storage is:

Mountpoint Backing storage Size Role / LVM on a 232 GiB RAID virtual disk 213 GiB operating system /DATA ext4 on a 7.3 TiB RAID virtual disk 7.3 TiB GPU-local staging and scratch

Do not write GPU workflows that assume /NVME_DATA1 exists. Use /DATA and stage durable results back to shared storage.

docs.title: Safe job pattern
docs.text:
1. Create a job-specific local directory.
2. Copy or link the required shared inputs.
3. Run high-I/O stages locally.
4. Verify final outputs.
5. Copy final outputs and logs to shared storage.
6. Remove local temporary data only after successful stage-out.

Include the Slurm job ID in scratch directory names to prevent two jobs from using the same path.

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
for PATHNAME in /DATA /NVME_DATA1 /NVME_DATA2 /NVME_DATA3; do
    findmnt -T "$PATHNAME"
done
df -hT /DATA /NVME_DATA1 /NVME_DATA2 /NVME_DATA3
df -ih /DATA /NVME_DATA1 /NVME_DATA2 /NVME_DATA3
nvme list
nvme smart-log /dev/nvmeX

For /DATA, inspect the RAID controller rather than treating the virtual /dev/sda device as a single physical disk.

docs.title: Shared Storage on Master
docs.text: master is both the cluster control point and the current shared-storage server. Its local filesystems must be healthy before workers attempt NFS mounts.

docs.title: Master filesystem map
docs.text:
Mountpoint Backing storage Filesystem Inventory capacity Role / RAID-controller virtual disk, partition 4 XFS 1.8 TiB operating system and /apps /home ZFS pool homefs, two 3.5 TiB Samsung NVMe members ZFS mirror 3.4 TiB usable user homes /nfs_master large SMC3108 virtual disk ext4 174 TiB active shared projects /Fungel large SMC3108 virtual disk ext4 212 TiB large shared datasets and archives

The inventory identifies controller virtual disks but not the underlying disk count or RAID level. Do not infer physical redundancy from /dev/sdX or the reported virtual-disk size; inspect the RAID controller separately.

docs.title: /home: ZFS on master, AutoFS on workers
docs.text:
The homefs pool is a mirror of:

nvme0n1
nvme1n1

ZFS mounts the dataset directly at /home on master. Master must not NFS-mount its own /home export over a 192.168.x.x address. A self-referential NFS mount can hide the real ZFS dataset and can block unrelated systemd services during startup.

Validate:

zpool status homefs
zfs list homefs
zfs get mounted,canmount,mountpoint homefs
findmnt -T /home

Expected source on master: homefs, not 192.168.x.2:/home.

docs.title: /nfs_master
docs.text:
This is the primary active shared project filesystem. The inventory captured it at approximately 96% usage, leaving about 8.5 TiB. That is a critical capacity condition, not comfortable free space for genomics pipelines whose temporary output may exceed their inputs.

The filesystem is mounted by UUID in /etc/fstab:

UUID=05daafa6-4248-4af9-9204-9468433879fb /nfs_master ext4 ...

docs.title: /Fungel
docs.text:
This large ext4 filesystem held approximately 144 TiB of 212 TiB in the inventory snapshot. It is intended for large shared datasets, references, and archive-oriented storage—not uncontrolled temporary output.

Its persistent identity is:

UUID=0c4d4acd-c77e-4bcd-9bcf-36037d372b00 /Fungel ext4 ...

docs.title: Why UUIDs matter
docs.text:
Large RAID virtual disks can change /dev/sda and /dev/sdb ordering after a reboot. FGHPC has observed these names swap while the filesystem UUIDs remained stable. Mount, diagnose, and document by UUID plus mountpoint—not by assuming that /dev/sda always means /nfs_master.

lsblk -f
blkid
findmnt -T /nfs_master
findmnt -T /Fungel

docs.title: /apps
docs.text:
/apps resides on the master's root filesystem rather than a separate large data disk. Workers receive the export as:

MASTER_DIRECT_IP:/apps → /nfsroot/apps

The inventory records the master root at only about 9% usage, but application growth still competes with operating-system space. Keep installers, caches, and temporary build trees out of /apps unless they are intentionally managed.

docs.title: Availability boundary
docs.text:
All four shared paths depend on master. The ZFS mirror and RAID controller may protect against some device failures, but they do not make the NFS service or master node highly available. A master outage removes these shared paths from all workers.

Redundancy is also not backup: deletion, corruption, and administrator mistakes can affect the live copy immediately.
